benchmarks.note: Land benchmarks: residential ¥/tsubo by station, adjusted from MLIT transactions via Utinokati and 2026 official points — read the adjustments, because the raw catchment averages describe a car city, not these walkable listings: JR Utsunomiya scored at ~40 for in-zone lots within a short walk (its multi-year catchment average is ~27 because the average transacted lot is a 33-minute walk); the LRT east side: Higashi-Shukugo/Eki-Higashiguchi ~40 (proxy; an official point at Higashi-Shukugo 3-chome prints 54.5), Yoto ~30 (proxy), Hiraishi/Yui-no-Mori-Nishi ~23, Kiyohara/the eastern terminus ~19–23 — the LRT opened in 2023 and its stop-level transaction series is still thin (~70 attributed deals), so every LRT figure is flagged lower-confidence. Tobu-Utsunomiya ~32 (proxy — no station transaction series exists), Tsuruta ~24 (district ~21, standard lots near the station ~26), Nishikawada ~19 (proxy), Suzumenomiya ~18 (official-point proxy), Okamoto ~17, Esoshima ~20 and Minami-Utsunomiya ~22 (proxies by position on the JR Nikko and Utsunomiya lines). Walk bands are nearly flat — land falls only ~9–12% per 10 minutes' walk here — except inside the LRT corridor's developed pockets, where values drop steeply beyond them. Used houses transacted at about ¥69万/tsubo standardised city-wide (floor-area basis; recent transaction averages 73–75): Wakamatsubara ~78 at the top, most established districts 66–78, and age bites hard (a 30-year-old house prices at ~46% of new per tsubo). Official residential land prices rose +1.2% in the 2026 公示地価 survey — the prefecture's all-use figure turned positive for the first time in 34 years — and the LRT corridor's residential point has risen ~3%/yr for five straight years.
